claims.text: There exists a Pulumi blog post titled "SST Runs on the Pulumi Engine: What It Means to Build on Pulumi" at /blog/sst-built-on-pulumi/ that covers the engine mechanics behind SST's migration to Pulumi.
Pulumi Crosswalk for AWS simplifies "day one" tasks, as described in the Pulumi AWS guide at /docs/iac/guides/clouds/aws/.
Pulumi offers an on-demand workshop titled "Getting Started with Infrastructure as Code on AWS" at https://www.pulumi.com/resources/getting-started-with-iac-pulumi-aws/.
Pulumi offers upcoming Platform Engineering or DevOps workshops listed at https://www.pulumi.com/resources/#upcoming.

Ion is the code name for a new engine for deploying SST applications, whose constructs are deployed using Pulumi instead of CDK and CloudFormation, and once Ion is stable it will be released as SST v3.
SST leverages Pulumi behind the scenes for its providers and deployment engine while also bridging Terraform providers through Pulumi.
SST (Serverless Stack) makes money primarily through its managed service called SST Console, which is optional and includes a free tier.
SST was originally built on top of AWS's Cloud Development Kit (CDK), which allowed developers to define their infrastructure using TypeScript or Python.
AWS CDK supports only AWS as a cloud provider (AWS-only), while Pulumi supports AWS, Azure, GCP, and on-premises infrastructure.
AWS CDK debugging is hard due to CloudFormation, while Pulumi offers real-time debugging.
AWS CDK supports only TypeScript and Python as languages, while Pulumi supports any programming language.
AWS CDK deployment speed is slower due to CloudFormation, while Pulumi offers faster direct execution.
AWS CDK's secrets management is limited to AWS Secrets Manager only, while Pulumi supports cross-cloud secret management.
AWS CDK's extensibility is limited to the AWS ecosystem, while Pulumi supports custom providers and workflows.
AWS CDK uses a CloudFormation state file for state management, while Pulumi uses Pulumi-managed state.
With CDK and CloudFormation, the infrastructure code is essentially a code generator producing an intermediary format such as YAML or JSON that is then executed to deploy resources.
Pulumi treats infrastructure code as a first-class program executed directly during deployment, instead of generating an intermediary format.

SST's Founding Engineer is quoted saying: "With Pulumi, the deployment process feels like a natural extension of writing code - it's intuitive and powerful and capable of advanced things that traditional IaC tools can't handle."
SST's shift from AWS CDK to Pulumi unlocks multi-cloud flexibility, faster deployments, and a better developer experience.
Pulumi lets SST offer a faster, more flexible, and provider-agnostic infrastructure experience.
SST v3 (the Ion-based rewrite) replaced AWS CDK and CloudFormation with an embedded Pulumi engine that calls Terraform-bridged providers to make the underlying cloud API calls.
Running `sst deploy` requires no separate Pulumi install and no Pulumi account.
SST's state is kept in an S3 bucket in the user's own AWS account.
SST's deployment engine has no Pulumi account or Pulumi Cloud dependency required.
Nitric runs application deployments through the Pulumi engine rather than building its own diff, state, and provider layer from scratch.
Defang runs application deployments through the Pulumi engine rather than building its own diff, state, and provider layer from scratch.
SST is still shipping (actively maintained) as of this writing.
The SST team's public attention has broadened to include an AI coding agent called opencode.
SST is an open source TypeScript framework for building and deploying full-stack applications to AWS and more than 150 other providers.
SST was formerly known as Serverless Stack.
Through 2023, SST's provisioning layer was built directly on AWS CDK and CloudFormation.
In late 2023 the SST team began a rewrite, code-named Ion, that replaced SST's entire deployment layer.
Ion shipped as SST v3 in mid-2024.
SST v3 (Ion) has been the only supported SST architecture since it shipped in mid-2024.

SST's blog post "Moving away from CDK" states: "Ion is a code name for a new engine for deploying SST applications. The constructs (or components) are defined using Terraform providers and deployed using Pulumi; as opposed to CDK and CloudFormation (CFN)."

SST's blog post "Moving away from CDK" states: "When you run `sst deploy`, those resources make a call to an embedded Pulumi engine that makes a call to their bridged Terraform provider, and this makes the AWS SDK calls to create your resources."
SST's docs page "What is SST" states: "SST uses Pulumi behind the scenes for the providers and the deployment engine. And Terraform's providers are bridged through Pulumi."

Gautier Blandin's article "Terraform, Pulumi, SST: a tradeoff analysis" states: "SST uses the Pulumi engine under the hood to manage and provision resources, and lets users write Pulumi code in addition to using SST's constructs, enabling resources with no associated SST constructs to still be defined and deployed."
Kiryl Anoshka's article "SST ditches AWS CDK. Time to move on to Ion" states: "You may notice right away the imports from Pulumi. It means the whole deployment process will be built on Pulumi now."

The published `package.json` for SST's platform package depends on `@pulumi/pulumi`, plus first-party Pulumi providers for AWS, Cloudflare, Docker builds, and more, alongside a Pulumiverse Vercel provider.
The `anomalyco/sst` GitHub repository was formerly named `sst/sst`.

The `platform/package.json` in the `anomalyco/sst` repository lists `@pulumi/pulumi`, `@pulumi/aws`, `@pulumi/cloudflare`, `@pulumi/command`, `@pulumi/docker-build`, `@pulumi/random`, `@pulumi/tls`, and `@pulumiverse/vercel` as direct dependencies, verified September 2026.
The Pulumi engine diffs desired state against actual state, builds a dependency graph, and orders operations.
Terraform-bridged providers translate each resource into cloud API calls.
Pulumi's Terraform bridge is Apache-2.0 licensed.
Pulumi's engine does not require a Pulumi account, a network call to Pulumi Cloud, or any Pulumi-hosted service to run.
Pulumi's Automation API works the same embeddable way, for teams embedding Pulumi programs inside their own tools.
The same Terraform provider bridge that SST uses lets any Pulumi user consume Terraform providers directly.
Nitric is a cloud-agnostic application framework.
Nitric's own docs state that "all of the direct deployment providers use Pulumi under the hood for their deployments."
Official Nitric providers are built directly on Pulumi's AWS, GCP, and Azure providers.
Defang deploys Docker Compose applications to the cloud.
Defang describes its Pulumi provider as taking "a Compose file, translates it to a Pulumi program, and runs `pulumi up`" to provision the result.
SST users are not Pulumi Cloud customers.
SST's state lives in the user's own S3 bucket, not in Pulumi's hosted service.
SST does not require a Pulumi account to work.
Most SST users never write a line of Pulumi code; they work entirely in SST's component model.
Because SST's constructs compile to Pulumi resources, resources that don't have a dedicated SST construct yet can still be defined directly in Pulumi and deployed as part of the same SST app.
The latest SST release, v4.17.1, went out in July 2026.
The `sst` package on npm is pulling roughly 796,000 downloads a week as of this writing.
npm download stats for `sst` show 796,291 downloads for the week of September 5-11, 2026.
SST's own team page credits the same team behind opencode.
opencode is an open source AI coding agent.
opencode has grown quickly since launch and now carries a larger following on GitHub than SST itself.
The `anomalyco/opencode` GitHub repository's star count was observed in September 2026 to exceed SST's own star count.
SST's release cadence and download numbers indicate SST is not being abandoned despite the team's broadened public attention.
The framework's dependency on the Pulumi engine hasn't changed as a result of the team's broadened public attention.
Pulumi Cloud provides cross-team visibility into infrastructure state.
Pulumi policy as code provides guardrails a platform team can enforce centrally.
Pulumi components enable sharing infrastructure patterns across a whole organization rather than just within one SST app.

Since SST v3 (the Ion rewrite, shipped mid-2024), `sst deploy` runs through an embedded Pulumi engine that calls Terraform-bridged providers to make the underlying cloud API calls, replacing SST's earlier architecture on AWS CDK and CloudFormation.
Pulumi's engine is embedded directly in the SST CLI.
Users don't need to install Pulumi separately or create a Pulumi account to deploy an SST app.
SST's components are defined using Terraform providers, but those providers are bridged through the Pulumi engine rather than run through Terraform itself.
SST does not invoke the Terraform CLI or write Terraform state.
The blog post "AWS CDK vs Pulumi: Why SST Chose Pulumi" tells the fuller story of SST's move off CDK, from SST's side.
The "How Pulumi IaC Works" doc page covers the engine mechanics referenced throughout this post.
The "Introducing: Support For Using Any Terraform Provider with Pulumi" post describes the bridge SST and others build on.
The Automation API page describes how other tools embed Pulumi the same way SST does.
SST is still maintained.

Reaching for Pulumi directly makes more sense once you need capabilities SST doesn't expose on its own, such as cross-team visibility, policy enforcement, or infrastructure shared across more than one application.
